title: Self-referential default arguments in three internal helpers
description:
Found this during my most recent [ry](https://github.com/sims1253/ry) audit


## Summary

Three internal helper functions declare **self-referential default
arguments** — a default that names the argument itself. When such a default
is actually evaluated, R raises:

```
Error: promise already under evaluation: recursive default argument reference or earlier problems?
```

The affected functions and signatures are:

```r
# R/step-join.R
dtplyr_auto_copy <- function(x, y, copy = copy) { ... }

# R/tidyeval-across.R
dt_squash_across <- function(call, env, data, j = j, is_top = TRUE) { ... }
dt_squash_if     <- function(call, env, data, j = j, reduce = "&") { ... }
```

## Latency

These are **latent** defects today: every current caller supplies the
argument, so the buggy defaults are never reached and there is no observable
runtime effect. Not sure if this is wanted behaviour for internal helpers.

- `dtplyr_auto_copy()` — sole caller is `step_join()`
  (`y <- dtplyr_auto_copy(x, y, copy = copy)`), which always forwards `copy`.
- `dt_squash_across()` — called by `capture_across()` and from `dt_squash()`
  (the `across`/`pick` branches); all pass `j`.
- `dt_squash_if()` — called by `capture_if_all()` and from `dt_squash()`
  (the `if_any`/`if_all` branches); all pass `j`.

## Reprex

```r
# define a function with the same self-referential default pattern
f <- function(x, y, copy = copy) force(copy)
f(1, 2)
#> Error: promise already under evaluation: recursive default argument reference or earlier problems?
```

The same error is raised by `dtplyr:::dtplyr_auto_copy()` when the `else`
branch (forwarding to `dplyr::auto_copy()`) is reached without an explicit
`copy`:

```r
library(dtplyr)
dt1 <- lazy_dt(data.frame(x = 1))
y <- structure(10, class = "foo")   # a non-data.frame, non-dtplyr_step object
dtplyr:::dtplyr_auto_copy(dt1, y)
#> Error: promise already under evaluation: recursive default argument reference or earlier problems?
```

title: Support nesting()
description:
Fixes #238.

`nesting()` needs to be treated separately from other variables in `expand()` and the resulting data.table code quickly gets a bit ugly, in particular as there is no nice support for a cross join by data.table.

TODO
* [ ] add tests
* [ ] handle factors
* [ ] add news
* [ ] check if row order is the same as for dataframe

## factors
> When used with factors, expand() uses the full set of levels, not just those that appear in the data. 

It is possible to handle factors the same way but not so nice because the type of a column is usually not known (respectively only when it wasn't mutated). I see two options to have the same behaviour for data.table as for dataframes:

* use `levels(x) %||% x` for every column. This is quite ugly
* define a special function and add it in front of the generated data.table code

title: mutate edge cases
description:
closes #321
closes #281

All the tests added to test-step-mutate.R result in an error on the main branch. These are all pretty rare use-cases, but trying to make dtplyr as compatible with existing working dplyr code as possible, even if it's a bit odd.

The changes are:

- Solved by `process_new_vars`
  - If there are **repeated variable names**, e.g. `mutate(dt, z = 2, z = 3)` this needs to be handled the same way nested arguments are handled on the main branch (even if there is no nesting) to avoid an error. `mutate_nested_vars` is renamed to `mutate_with_braces` because it's= now not only used when arguments are nested.
    - [test](https://github.com/tidyverse/dtplyr/pull/324/files#diff-68dfa5e2cb0290c32457805c202b1e388a6823e6dabaeacaa3f9f4fd13f4ef13R73)
  - If there is a **variable removal**, i.e. a mutate argument `var = NULL` not followed by any other mutate arguments named `var` (e.g. not `var = NULL, var = 3`), then that variable should not be in the final output.
    - If the data is grouped, you need an additional step (`[.data.table` call) to remove the variable because `DT[, var := NULL, by = g]` results in an error.
    - If we are in a `mutate_with_braces` branch, it's hard to determine how you should modify the current `j` expression to get the correct output. Some things that seem like they should work don't, see example below. So to keep things simple, this case is handled the same as grouped data, i.e. an extra `[.data.table` call is added.
    - [test](https://github.com/tidyverse/dtplyr/pull/324/files#diff-68dfa5e2cb0290c32457805c202b1e388a6823e6dabaeacaa3f9f4fd13f4ef13R159)
 
 ```{r}

dd <- data.table(x = 1)
dd[, c('z', 'x') := {x <- NULL; list(2, NULL)}][]
#>        x     z
#>    <num> <num>
#> 1:     2     2
```

title: slice_max() and slice_min() speed
description:
Fixes #216 and #218.

The translation

``` r
library(data.table)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(dtplyr)

DT <- rbindlist(rep(list(mtcars), 10e3), idcol = "id")
DF <- as_tibble(DT)

DT %>% 
  lazy_dt("DT") %>% 
  group_by(id) %>% 
  slice_max(mpg, n = 2) %>% 
  show_query()
#> DT[DT[, .I[rank(desc(mpg), ties.method = "min", na.last = "keep") <= 2L], by = .(id)]$V1][order(id, desc(mpg))]

DT %>% 
  lazy_dt("DT") %>% 
  group_by(id) %>% 
  slice_max(mpg, n = 2, with_ties = FALSE) %>% 
  show_query()
#> DT[DT[, .I[rank(desc(mpg), ties.method = "first", na.last = "keep") <= 2L], by = .(id)]$V1][order(id, desc(mpg))]
```

<sup>Created on 2021-03-05 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v1.0.0)</sup>

The following code might be a bit more efficient

```r
DT[DT[order(id, desc(mpg)), .I[rank(desc(mpg), ties.method = "first", na.last = "keep") <= 2L], by = .(id)]$V1]
```

I had it in the beginning but this would require an additional argument to `step_subset_i()` and I wasn't sure whether the extra complexity is worth it.

~Interestingly, `with_ties = FALSE` is slower. This is due to `rank("min")` being much faster than `rank("first")`.~ (I cannot reproduce this anymore)

library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(dtplyr)
# devtools::load_all(".")

  dplyr = DF %>% 
    group_by(id) %>% 
    slice_max(mpg, n = 2) %>% 
    ungroup(),
  dtplyr = DT %>% 
    group_by(id) %>%

title: Implement pivot_wider()
description:
Implements `pivot_wider()` for use on lazy data.tables.

A few notes:
* For `names_repair` to be an option, `.name_repair` needed to be exposed in `as_tibble.dtplyr_step()`. It doesn't break any tests, but `print.dtplyr_step()` and `dtplyr:::simulate_vars()` no longer do checks for valid names.
* I used `lapply()` & `vapply()` - not sure if you'd rather use [compat-purrr.R](https://github.com/r-lib/rlang/blob/master/R/compat-purrr.R) instead.
* It currently doesn't work with `".value"` in `names_from`. I'm not positive what the logic is for that.
* All tests are taken from the tidyr version. It works in all cases except for 3 that are commented out:
  - One with `".value"` usage
  - One that deals with data frame columns
  - One that returns a list column
* In the case of multiple `names_from` columns or in the case that `names_glue` is used, deep copies are made when using `mutate()` to help extract the new column names. This could be made faster by using [data.table's shallow copy trick.](https://github.com/Rdatatable/data.table/issues/3214#issuecomment-462490046)
According to Matt Dowle it is supposed to be supported until they export `shallow()`. Not sure your opinion on that. `pivot_wider()` works as is, or a simple internal `shallow_dt <- function(x) filter(x, TRUE)` could be used here.

If you have any changes you want me to make let me know. Also feel free to make changes yourself if you want.

title: Adds dt_pivot_wider() function that emulates tidyr::pivot_wider()
description:
- Attempts to follow the same implementation pattern for a new `step`.  This way it can be used in combination with other converted `dplyr` verbs:
  - Implements a new `step` via `step_pivot_wider()`, which contains the `new_step()` call
  - Implements a new `step_call()`,  with `dt_call.dtplyr_step_pivot_wider()`, which contains the actual `data.table` code that will be used
  - Implements `dt_pivot_wider()` which creates the step in for a lazy_dt()`
- Uses `data.table::dcast()` to perform the pivoting
- Documents function in order to avoid depending on `tidyr`'s help docs
- Names the function `dt_pivot_wider()`, and not `pivot_wider()`, to follow the same pattern as `dbplyr`: https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/pull/344
- Emulates most of the tests `pivot_wider()` runs through in `tidyr`.  The new script has 100% coverage.
```
library(data.table)
library(tidyr)
library(dtplyr)
library(dplyr)

us_rent_income %>%
  as.data.table() %>%
  lazy_dt() %>%
  filter(as.integer(GEOID) < 5) %>%
  dt_pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = c(estimate, moe), names_sep = "-") %>%
  filter(NAME == "Alaska")

#> Source: local data table [?? x 5]
#> Call:   dcast(data = `_DT1`[as.integer(GEOID) < 5], formula = GEOID + 
#>     NAME ~ variable, value.var = c(estimate = "estimate", moe = "moe"
#> ), fill = NULL, sep = "-")[NAME == "Alaska"]
#> 
#>   GEOID NAME   `estimate-income` `estimate-rent` `moe-income` `moe-rent`
#>   <chr> <chr>              <dbl>           <dbl>        <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1 02    Alaska             32940            1200          508         13
#> 
#> # Use as.data.table()/as.data.frame()/as_tibble() to access results
```

A possible issue is that when there are only two columns in a data set, the pivoting adds a field called `.`.  When collected into `tibble` it creates a variable column, not sure if that's acceptable or not: 

```
tibble(key = c("x", "y", "z"), val = 1:3) %>%
  as.data.table() %>%
  lazy_dt() %>%
  dt_pivot_wider(names_from = key, values_from = val) %>%
  as_tibble()
#> # A tibble: 1 x 4
#>   .         x     y     z
#>   <chr> <int> <int> <int>
#> 1 .         1     2     3
```

title: Join using merge
description:
In data.table v1.9.6, `merge.data.table` has gained a `by.x` and `by.y` argument. Also it does not copy anymore, and does not need a key, so using `merge` to perform joins should be more efficient and more convenient.

From `?merge.data.table`:

> In versions <= v1.9.4, if the specified columns in by was not the key (or head of the key) of x or y, then a copy is first rekeyed prior to performing the merge. This was less performant and memory inefficient. The concept of secondary keys (implemented in v1.9.4) was used to overcome this limitation from v1.9.6+. No deep copies are made anymore and therefore very performant and memory efficient. Also there is better control for providing the columns to merge on with the help of newly implemented by.x and by.y arguments.

Using column renaming and the `on =` argument for non-`merge` joins, `semi_join.data.table` and `anti_join.data.table`, saves the need for `setkey` and copying.

This should fix #20, #21.

@krlmlr, we checked this out together, you may have another look. I had to remove some `with = FALSE`, which only work for the `j`, not for the `i` argument. But also without `with = FALSE`, the current solution works if a column is named `y_labels`, so we should be fine. Also `nomatch = 0L` cannot be used in an anti join.
